name: Erik Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik Baker, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know the Old Market circuit well, though I'm on the lower pay scale; I enjoy finding a physical fault, and I sometimes use the approved AI helper to tidy notes after the crew has finished.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The annual car insurance took nearly all our savings. My partner Tessa works variable hours at a dental reception desk, and our grown children are paying their own bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker report is useful after a late repair, but the pole still needs testing. I'd rather save ten minutes at a desk than rush one minute with a live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I already watch the account each week. My pay is low for this trade, the yearly car insurance used our savings, and Tessa's dental reception shifts change when appointments are light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my normal repair shifts and ask whether the depot has safe weekend callouts this month. In the first year Tessa and I would stop the garden-centre trips until we have a month's rent set aside; I'd use the approved AI note helper only after repairs, as I sometimes do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel sound at work and stretched at home. Our grown children visit, but they have their own bills and can't be our emergency fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened on the last late repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Old Market transformer had a loose lead and the label was greasy. I measured twice, then wrote the correct circuit number before anyone closed the cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the note helper ever help with safety?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps me remember the order of events, but I check it against the signed sheet. I wouldn't ask it whether a line was dead.

say: I'd welcome **quicker reports** after safe repairs.
I'd say **live-line testing** cannot be rushed to save desk time.
think: Our **car insurance** used the reserve while my line pay remains low.
Tessa's **variable reception shifts** make the weekly account balance uncomfortable.
do: Keep **normal repair shifts** and ask about safe weekend callouts.
Pause **garden-centre trips** until one month's rent is saved; use approved AI notes only after repairs.
feel: **Sound** in field work, stretched by household money.
S0.quote: I'd rather save ten minutes at a desk than rush one minute with a live line.
fieldNote: Erik's **baseline anxiety** comes from low pay, car insurance and Tessa's varying hours even in a quiet AI picture.
His **occasional AI notes** follow physical checks and the signed circuit record, never decide whether a line is dead.

steps.text: Continue paid repair shifts and ask about safe weekend callouts
Pause garden-centre trips until one month of rent is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office to let the dental receptionists and our dispatchers test customer and route software before changing jobs. A fast answer is no help if the wrong patient or circuit is on the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My line work should last for now, but Tessa answers calls and books appointments, so her hours could fall soon. If dispatch tightens, I may lose weekend callouts as well, and we have less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the dispatcher to compare the approved route tool with the Old Market feeder sheet after a real trial. In the first year Tessa and I would postpone replacing our sofa if either pay packet shrinks, and I'd ask her clinic about paid time to learn the new booking system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious for Tessa and watchful about my own extra hours. I'm willing to use a proven map, but a tidy screen isn't a safety check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could a route trial miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Market has two service doors with the same number; only the rear door reaches the transformer. Our dispatcher knows which one the truck needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid learning mean for Tessa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She could train while still bringing home wages. We can't afford a week off for an unpaid course when the rent is due.

say: I'd seek **worker trials** before booking and dispatch software change jobs.
I'd check **patient and circuit details** rather than trusting quick screen answers.
think: Tessa's **appointment hours** could fall as AI answers calls.
My **weekend callouts** could also shrink, with under a month saved.
do: Compare the **approved route tool** with the Old Market feeder sheet after trials.
Delay the **sofa replacement** if pay shrinks and ask the clinic about paid booking training.
feel: **Anxious** for Tessa, watchful about my extra hours.
S1.quote: We can't afford a week off for an unpaid course when the rent is due.
fieldNote: Erik sees **early household exposure** through Tessa's dental reception work and a possible cut to his callout pay.
He wants **paid clinic training** for Tessa and checks field routes against a specific two-door transformer site.

steps.text: Use the approved route tool after trials and check Old Market feeder records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 could take booking work first, while robots reaching repairs around 2031 threaten our crew. We need a public staffing timetable and paid inspection training before either set of workers is left guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when field robots arrive, and I expect a large cut in repair hours. Tessa may already have fewer clinic shifts, our reserve is under a month, and there are only a couple of line employers close enough to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the company for a written robot plan and ask the employment office what paid electrical inspection courses exist. In 2029 I'd enroll if the course pays wages; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for every posted inspection shift nearby and ask our grown daughter for help finding train times to distant interviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wake at night counting rent against the hours we might both lose. I can learn a proven inspection method, but I can't invent a local employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your daughter do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter could help find a route and maybe drive us to the station. I'd pay my own fare if I could; her income is for her own home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the depot early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the paid shifts are the only bridge we have right now. I'd apply while still repairing lines, not resign to chase a course title.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 booking AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd demand a **written staffing timetable** and paid inspection training.
think: At **63**, I expect a large loss of repair hours.
Tessa's **clinic shifts** may already shrink while our reserve is nearly empty.
do: Request a **robot staffing plan** and paid-course information now.
Enroll if **training pays wages** in 2029, then apply for posted inspection shifts in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over two likely income cuts and scarce local employers.
S2.quote: I can learn a proven inspection method, but I can't invent a local employer.
fieldNote: Erik expects **major hour losses** by 2031 after possible clinic cuts and says he wakes at night over rent.
His **training choice** depends on continued wages; his daughter offers travel information, not household income.

steps.text: Request the written company robot staffing plan
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if wages continue
Apply for posted inspection shifts while retaining depot pay
Ask his grown daughter to help plan travel for distant interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers five years gives them time to test robots in real weather and show crews the pay for any new role. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, and field robots follow around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement at 66 could be possible, but we have almost nothing saved and I don't know the pension amount. Tessa's appointment work could change in 2031, so a plan based on today's two payslips would be shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request a written pension forecast and ask the depot for records of robot trial failures. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if one is offered; in 2034 I'd compare the actual inspection wage with rent and medicine before deciding whether to keep working or retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a bit more room to plan, though not much money to use that room. I want numbers and a real trial, not a promise that the new job will be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which trial failure would you look for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether the robot notices a greasy label on the Old Market transformer and stops for a human check. The wrong circuit there could hurt somebody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is too small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep safe paid line shifts if the company still has them and apply for posted inspection work. I can't stop earning because a calendar says 66.

say: I'd request **real-weather trials** and actual pay for new roles.
I'd separate **2031 thinking AI** from 2034 repair robots.
think: Retirement at **66** needs a pension figure and household budget.
Tessa's **booking income** might fall before field robots arrive.
do: Get a **pension forecast** and review robot trial failures this year.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; compare real inspection wages with rent in 2034.
feel: **Some room** to plan, limited by a near-empty account.
S3.quote: I can't stop earning because a calendar says 66.
fieldNote: Erik's **2034 choice** depends on verified pension and inspection pay, with Tessa's earlier booking exposure in the budget.
He would **test a greasy-label failure** at Old Market and keep paid shifts if retirement remains unaffordable.

steps.text: Get a written pension forecast and review robot trial failures
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if one opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew ten years is enough to write down the odd faults before a machine becomes the usual repairer. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to retire before 71, but a hope isn't the pension statement. The car insurance comes round every year, and Tessa's reception pay could change before robots reach the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep earning line wages and request pension figures, then rebuild a small cash reserve after the insurance bill. In 2037 Tessa and I would set a retirement date only if low-hours income covers rent; if it doesn't, I'd apply for a posted inspection job before the 2039 robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less threatened by the robot date and still worried about this year's bills. A decade helps us prepare only if the wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the next insurance payment is covered, I'd transfer eighteen from each actual weekend callout. I won't put imaginary extra shifts into the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What notes would you leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mark the greasy label and rear service door at Old Market on the crew sheet. A new worker can check the site before trusting a clean map.

I'd note **2039 robots** reach repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** requires a real pension statement.
Tessa's **reception pay** and annual insurance cost remain household risks.
do: Keep **paid line work** and request pension figures now.
Save **eighteen from real callouts** after insurance is covered, then review retirement in 2037.
feel: **Less threatened** by robots, still worried about present bills.
S4.quote: I won't put imaginary extra shifts into the budget.
fieldNote: Erik's **distant robot date** gives planning time but does not remove annual insurance costs or Tessa's possible income loss.
His **saving step** starts after the insurance bill and uses real weekend callouts rather than projected pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Tessa's booking hours could shrink first and 2031 robots could cut my repair shifts. I need a written staffing plan, paid inspection training, real vacancies and help reaching distant interviews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what the new inspection shift actually pays. A new title won't cover rent if the hours disappear.

headlineQuote: A new title won't cover rent if the hours disappear.
portrait: Erik is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, low pay and less than one month saved.
His **annual insurance bill** emptied the reserve, while Tessa's variable dental reception hours make household income uncertain.
He uses **AI occasionally** after repairs and will adopt route tools only after real trials and circuit checks.
The **2031 robot date** alarms him because Tessa's booking work may shrink first and he expects major crew-hour losses.
More warning permits **pension checks** from real callouts while he keeps paid repairs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Erik most because booking AI could cut Tessa's hours before 2031 robots cut his shifts.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **written staffing plan**, paid inspection training, actual vacancies and interview travel help.
